The Maestro · Part 3 · Phase 0 · 💼 Founder hat

The Plan and the Money

Part 2 built a training stack Gopala trusts and, in the scenario, tests showing the self-improving idea survives contact with real models. Now Gopala has to decide what that idea is worth spending money on, and how much. Should he pre-train his own model from scratch or post-train an open one? How big, on how many GPUs, for how long? Rent or buy? How much must he raise, and how long will it last? This part answers those questions from first principles, with a script anyone can rerun with their own numbers, and ends with an 18-month master plan and the one-page memo he takes to investors.

2. The big decision

Four ways to get a model: cost including experiments

A · post-train open 32B$0.80M
B · 8B dense from scratch$5.34M
D · MoE 12B active from scratch$7.25M
C · 32B dense from scratch$9.29M

Real output of budget.py (our assumptions: 30% MFU, $2.35/GPU-hr ⚠️).

  • There are only four sensible ways for a start-up to get the model at the centre of its product.
    • Gopala writes them down as scenarios with explicit sizes, so the comparison is about numbers, not taste.
ScenarioWhat it meansUpsideDownside
A · Post-train an open 32BTake an open-weight model; fine-tune and run reinforcement learning on verified skillsCheap, fast, strong from day oneSomeone else's architecture, data and licence; competitors can start from the same base
B · From scratch, 8B densePre-train a small dense model on ~15T tokens (Llama-3-8B-like data scale)Full ownership; cheap to serveSmall; general ability below good open models
C · From scratch, 32B denseA mid-size dense model on ~6T tokensStronger, still simple to trainMost expensive to train and to serve
D · From scratch, MoE with 12B activeA mixture-of-experts model (larger total, 12B active per token) on ~10T tokensBig-model quality at small-model serving cost (the DeepSeek-V3 lesson)Harder to train well; lower utilisation; more engineering

3. Compute from first principles

Compute from first principles

🔢FLOPs6 × parameters × tokens
⚡GPU speed989 TFLOP/s peak × 30% MFU
⏱️GPU-hoursFLOPs ÷ speed, +10% failures
💵CostGPU-hours × $/hour

The same four steps price every option in the table below.

Every number in this part comes from three rules of thumb, explained in the site's frontier-lab start-up playbook and planning the Llama 3 run:

Training ≈ 6 · N · DFLOPs to train a dense transformer with N parameters on D tokens: about 2 for the forward pass and 4 for the backward pass, per parameter per token. For mixture-of-experts, N is the active parameters.
Generation ≈ 2 · N · DProducing D tokens (for example reinforcement-learning rollouts) costs a forward pass only. It runs at lower utilisation than training.
GPU-time = FLOPs ÷ (peak · MFU)An H100 peaks at 989 TFLOP/s in dense BF16 (NVIDIA spec). Real training achieves 30–45% of that ("model FLOPs utilisation"); the rest is lost to communication, memory and waiting.
  • On top of the final run, two multipliers dominate the real bill:
    • experiments (small runs, ablations, data mixes, failed attempts
    • labs commonly spend several times the final run) and failures (Llama 3's 405B run saw 466 interruptions in 54 days
    • see running the run).

4. The budget script

budget.py · Python 3, no dependencies
"""budget.py — the Maestro's compute and cash plan, from first principles.

Training compute  ≈ 6 · N_active · D        (dense or MoE active params, tokens)
Generation (RL)   ≈ 2 · N_active · D_gen    (rollouts are inference)
GPU-seconds       = FLOPs / (peak FLOP/s · MFU)
All prices and efficiencies are ASSUMPTIONS you should replace with real quotes.

  python3 budget.py
"""

H100_BF16 = 989e12          # NVIDIA H100 SXM dense BF16 peak, FLOP/s (spec sheet)
PRICE = 2.35                # $/GPU-hour, 1-year reserved H100 (secondary report, Mar 2026) — assumption
GPUS = 1024                 # cluster size for the main run

SCENARIOS = [
    # name, active params, train tokens, MFU, RL rollout tokens, experiment multiplier
    ("A  post-train open 32B",          32e9, 0.1e12, 0.40, 1.0e12, 2.0),
    ("B  from scratch 8B dense",         8e9, 15e12,  0.40, 0.5e12, 3.0),
    ("C  from scratch 32B dense",       32e9,  6e12,  0.40, 1.0e12, 3.0),
    ("D  from scratch MoE 12B active",  12e9, 10e12,  0.30, 0.8e12, 3.0),
]
FAILURE_OVERHEAD = 0.10     # restarts, lost steps, bad nodes (Llama 3 saw 466 interruptions in 54 days)
RL_MFU = 0.20               # generation runs at lower utilisation than training


def plan(name, n, d, mfu, d_gen, exp_mult):
    train_flops = 6 * n * d
    gen_flops = 2 * n * d_gen
    gpu_h = (train_flops / (H100_BF16 * mfu) + gen_flops / (H100_BF16 * RL_MFU)) / 3600
    gpu_h *= 1 + FAILURE_OVERHEAD
    days = gpu_h / GPUS / 24
    final = gpu_h * PRICE
    total = final * (1 + exp_mult)          # experiments, ablations, evals cost a multiple of the final run
    return train_flops, gpu_h, days, final, total


print(f"{'scenario':34s} {'train FLOPs':>11s} {'GPU-hours':>10s} {'days@'+str(GPUS):>9s} {'final run':>10s} {'with R&D':>10s}")
for s in SCENARIOS:
    f, h, dys, fin, tot = plan(*s)
    print(f"{s[0]:34s} {f:11.2e} {h:10,.0f} {dys:9.1f} ${fin/1e6:8.2f}M ${tot/1e6:8.2f}M")

# Runway: compute is the biggest line, but not the only one
monthly_people = 150_000     # Gopala, contractors (DC technicians, security, legal), agent API bills (assumption)
monthly_serving = 64 * PRICE * 24 * 30   # a 64-GPU serving cluster for design partners
monthly_other = 60_000       # storage, egress, data licences, tools, insurance (assumption)
raise_usd = 20e6
compute_total = plan(*SCENARIOS[0])[4] + plan(*SCENARIOS[3])[4]     # the hybrid plan: A now, D later
burn = monthly_people + monthly_serving + monthly_other
months = (raise_usd - compute_total) / burn
print(f"\nhybrid plan (A then D): training compute ${compute_total/1e6:.1f}M of a ${raise_usd/1e6:.0f}M raise")
print(f"monthly burn besides training: ${burn/1e3:,.0f}k (people ${monthly_people/1e3:,.0f}k, "
      f"serving ${monthly_serving/1e3:,.0f}k, other ${monthly_other/1e3:,.0f}k) → ~{months:.0f} months of runway")
$ python3 budget.py scenario train FLOPs GPU-hours days@1024 final run with R&D A post-train open 32B 1.92e+22 113,695 4.6 $ 0.27M $ 0.80M B from scratch 8B dense 7.20e+23 568,475 23.1 $ 1.34M $ 5.34M C from scratch 32B dense 1.15e+24 988,653 40.2 $ 2.32M $ 9.29M D from scratch MoE 12B active 7.20e+23 771,149 31.4 $ 1.81M $ 7.25M hybrid plan (A then D): training compute $8.1M of a $20M raise monthly burn besides training: $318k (people $150k, serving $108k, other $60k) → ~38 months of runway
  • Three things stand out.
    • Post-training an open model costs about a tenth of any from-scratch option.
    • A from-scratch run at start-up scale is a month on 1,024 GPUs and a few million dollars for the final run, but five to nine million once experiments and failures are counted.
    • And the MoE option buys a model with far more total capacity than the 8B dense one for about 35% more compute, because the cost follows active parameters while the quality follows total parameters more closely.

6. The choice: a hybrid plan

The hybrid plan

🚀Maestro-0Post-train an open model, ship to partners (months 3–6)
🗃️Verified dataReal client tasks feed the skill library
🏗️Maestro-1Pre-train own 12B-active MoE (months 9–10.5)
🔁FlywheelPost-training and the RSI loop (months 10.5+)

Ship first to earn the data; then train the model that only that data makes possible.

Part 1 concluded that the moat is verified data and the gate, not the technique. That settles the order of play:

Now: Maestro-0 (scenario A)Post-train a strong open model on the skill loop and ship it to design partners within the first months. Purpose: real clients, real verified data, revenue, and proof that the loop works on production tasks.
Next: Maestro-1 (scenario D)Pre-train a mixture-of-experts model from scratch, with an architecture and tokenizer designed for code and tools, trained on public data plus the verified-skill data that only Gopala has. Purpose: full ownership of weights and licence, cheaper serving, and a base model whose data rights are clean.
  • Why not just stay on an open model?
    • Three reasons, all about the moat:
      • the licence and future direction of someone else's model are outside his control
      • the data mix of a model he did not train is unknown, which complicates the contamination checks his evaluations depend on (Evaluation Layer Part 2)
      • a model trained from the start on verified skills should absorb them better than one fine-tuned at the end (H2, to be tested in Phase 2).
    • Why not pre-train first?
    • Because it would burn the most money before a single client proves the idea.
  • The honest caveat: a 12B-active model trained by one start-up will not beat the frontier labs' best general models.
    • It does not need to.
    • It needs to be the best model for its clients' verified work, at a serving cost they can afford.

7. Sizing the from-scratch model

  • The Chinchilla study found that, for a fixed training budget, about 20 tokens per parameter minimises loss.
    • Modern models deliberately train far beyond that (Llama 3 8B saw about 15 trillion tokens), because a smaller model trained longer is cheaper to serve for its whole life.
    • Gopala follows the modern practice: the serving bill, not the training bill, dominates a product company's costs over time (the Great Flip).
ChoiceMaestro-1 planReason
ArchitectureMixture-of-experts, 12B active parametersQuality per serving dollar
Tokens~10T: filtered web, code, maths, documentation, plus verified skillsOpen corpora alone reach this scale; FineWeb alone is ~15T tokens of English web text
ContextLong context added in a late training stageCheaper than training long from the start (Llama 3's approach)
PrecisionBF16 with FP8 matmuls where stableSpeed; FP8 needs care (ML Layer Part 4)
Compute~7.2 × 1023 FLOPs; ~31 days on 1,024 H100-class GPUs at 30% MFUFrom budget.py

8. Rent or buy?

  • Buying 1,024 GPUs means paying for the chips (H100 prices have been widely reported in the tens of thousands of dollars each ⚠️), plus servers, networking, storage, a data hall with liquid-cooling-capable power and staff to run it, all before training starts.
    • The final run itself needs those GPUs for about a month.
    • The AI Factory as a Service economics calculator shows the break-even for owning usually needs high utilisation over years.
    • For a start-up with one big run, a stream of experiments and an uncertain future, renting wins on every count: speed, cash and flexibility.
Rent the training clusterReserve 1,024 GPUs for ~2 months around the main run; use smaller on-demand slices for experiments (neoclouds or hyperscalers).
Rent the serving cluster64 GPUs reserved for design partners, scaled with demand.
Revisit ownership at scaleOnly when utilisation is high and predictable for years: the future "full frontier" section of this site.
  • Renting does not remove Phase 1's work, it changes it: Gopala still has to choose and contract the provider, verify the cluster on day zero, install his own software stack and run operations.
    • Parts 4–7 cover exactly that.

11. The investor memo

Maestro · Seed memo · one page

Problem

Companies want AI that does real engineering work reliably. General models are impressive but do not learn from a company's own work, and their improvements are not auditable.

Insight

In domains where success can be checked by machine, a model can keep and reuse its verified solutions, and fold the best into its weights, under a fixed, auditable gate (an L4 self-improving system).

Evidence so far

A controlled toy experiment (Part 1, real) and pre-registered real-model tests (Part 2; in our scenario they come out positive) show retrieved, gated skills raise success at equal compute; naive memory makes things worse, which is why the gate matters.

Moat

Proprietary verified-skill data that compounds with every client task, and a gate clients and regulators can audit. Not the technique itself.

Plan

Maestro-0 on a post-trained open model for design partners now; Maestro-1, our own mixture-of-experts model, pre-trained from month 9.

Use of funds ($20M)

~$8M training compute, ~$4M serving, ~$5M people and contractors, ~$3M data, safety, legal and reserve.

Biggest risks

Big labs focusing on this niche; clients unwilling to share tasks; the loop drifting or gaming its checks (mitigated by the gate, external evaluations and human sign-off).

15. Reading the numbers

Primary / standard
H100 SXM dense BF16 peak 989 TFLOP/s (NVIDIA). 6·N·D and 2·N·D approximations (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022). Chinchilla ~20 tokens per parameter. Llama 3: 8B trained on ~15T tokens; 466 interruptions in 54 days for 405B (Meta). FineWeb ~15T tokens (Hugging Face).
Secondary ⚠️
$2.35 per H100-hour on one-year contracts (SemiAnalysis figure reported by secondary sources, March 2026); H100 purchase prices.
Our assumptions
Scenario sizes, MFU, failure overhead, experiment multipliers, salaries, serving cluster, the $20M raise, gates and plan.
